title: Batching config entropy — debug log
content:
Quick summary:
- Weird drop in sustained QPS on staging (svc: chat-infer-stg) after the 2026-01-30 push. Client latency p50 unchanged, but p95/p99 and overall tokens/sec down ~35%.
- Symptoms: batches are often size=1; batching window metric 'batch_wait_ms' shows steady increase. KV-cache hit ratio slightly lower (down ~6ppt). No obvious GPU saturation.
- Hypothesis: configuration/environment drift caused batching deadlines to be shorter or continuous-batcher to fall back to immediate dispatch (edge case when deadline calc overflows or ticker fired too frequently). Also possible: new instrumented metric changed scheduling (observation side-effect).

What I observed (raw):
- Baseline (2026-01-29, before push): tokens/sec ~ 124k, mean batch_size 6.1, percent singleton batches ~ 8%
- After (2026-02-02): tokens/sec ~ 81k, mean batch_size 2.7, singleton batches ~ 44%

Commands & probes I ran (most useful first):
- curl to runtime metrics endpoint:
  curl -sS http://stg-metrics.internal:9090/metrics | rg batch | sed -n '1,120p'
  (grabbed batch_wait_ms, batch_size_histogram, batch_dispatch_count)
- k exec into one pod and stream logs while exercising traffic with ab (client):
  ab -n 20000 -c 200 -p small_payload.json -T 'application/json' http://chat-infer-stg:8080/v1/generate
- toggled continuous-batcher flags on one replica via /admin/config:
  PATCH /admin/config {"continuous_batcher.enabled": false}  -> no perf improvement (makes behavior worse: token/sec drops further)
  PATCH /admin/config {"continuous_batcher.enabled": true, "continuous_batcher.default_deadline_ms": 6} -> partial recovery (batch_size to ~4)
- compared env from last-good image vs current image:
  kubectl get pod -o yaml | rg -A2 CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_  -> found CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS=6 on good, absent on new (defaults to 1 in code)

Error snippets and log fragments (redacted):
- continuous-batcher WARN: deadline-calc overflow, using fallback=1ms at 2026-02-01T18:03:12Z
- router INFO: dispatched batch size=1 reason=deadline-expired route=short-seq at 2026-02-01T18:03:12Z
- kv-cache DEBUG: lookup miss (key=...); cause=kv-prefix-eviction?
- scheduler ERROR: ticker scheduling missed tick (delta=120ms) 2026-02-01T18:03:12.121Z

Environment diff (what changed between deployments):
- build 2026-01-29 -> env var CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS explicitly set to 6 in deployment manifest.
- build 2026-01-30 -> removed the env var in a refactor (moved to feature flags service). New runtime code path reads from remote flags; fallback returns 1ms on timeout. Feature flag service rollout was partial in staging (rate-limited).
- metrics exporter instrumentation added a small blocking step in the batching hot path (a synchronous gauge update) in PR #341 (linked) — could add 50–100us to batch scheduling loop and push some batches to deadline expiry sooner.

What seems most plausible (synthesizing):
1) ENV/flag removal -> continuous-batcher saw deadline drop from 6ms -> 1ms for some pods. With deadline=1ms many requests leave as singletons.
2) Instrumentation + GC pauses + scheduler tick jitter -> combined with short deadline magnifies singleton percentage.
3) KV cache miss rate increase is downstream effect (smaller batches less likely to hit prefix cache).

Experiments to validate (I already did some):
- Re-add env var to one node group (k patch deployment to include CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS=6), observe batch histograms — result: batch_size increased from 2.7 -> 5.0 within 90s. This is strong evidence.
- Remove blocking metric update from the hot path in a local build and run microbench: results show ~80us lower scheduling latency.
- Ramp traffic with long-seq synthetic to measure cache hit correlation to batch size. (planned)

Immediate mitigation (runbook style):
- Roll single replica group with env var back to 6ms (hotfix) and monitor tokens/sec and p99.
- Revert PR #341 instrumentation or change it to async non-blocking gauge push.
- Add defensive fallback in continuous-batcher: if deadline < 2ms, cap to min(4ms) and emit alert.

Longer-term / follow-ups:
- Add integration test that asserts average batch_size >= 4 under synthetic 100qps workload (to catch flag misconfig).
- Add alert when median batch_wait_ms > expected by >2x for 5m window.
- Audit all feature-flag transitions that replace env-configs to ensure rollout atomicity.
- Document hot-path invariants in serving-runtime README.

Notes / things I still want to check:
- Confirm whether any other pods got CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS removed in other environments (prod?).
- Check if the feature flag client had any error logs/timeouts around 2026-01-30 (I saw ~30s window of timeouts in ff-client).
- Whether autoscaler induced pod churn at the same time causing transient misbalanced groups.

Payloads / commands to reproduce locally (dev laptop):
1) Start local minimal runtime with continuous-batcher enabled and an env var DEADLINE=1ms: 
   export CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS=1 && ./run-local --mini
   ./bench-client -qps 200 -concurrency 50 -seq-len-dist "short:0.85,long:0.15"
2) Toggle env var to 6ms and compare ./bench-client histograms.

Quick todo (my next steps):
- [ ] Patch staging deployment to set env var to 6ms for all replicas (in progress).
- [ ] Create tiny PR to make gauge update async (codeowner: Marco).
- [ ] Add small assertion test in e2e-batching-tests.
- [ ] Add an incident note to SERVE-4821 with summary and link to this doc.

If anyone is reading — feel free to ping me for help reproing locally. Leaving the k8s commands I used appended below.

Appendix — useful commands (copied from session):
- kubectl rollout restart deploy/chat-infer-stg -n staging
- kubectl set env deploy/chat-infer-stg CONTINUOUS_BATCHER_DEADLINE_MS=6 -n staging
- kubectl logs -f deploy/chat-infer-stg -c runtime | rg "continuous-batcher|deadline|dispatch" --line-buffered
- ab -n 20000 -c 200 -p small_payload.json -T 'application/json' http://chat-infer-stg:8080/v1/generate
- curl -sS http://stg-metrics.internal:9090/metrics | rg batch_wait_ms -n

End of scratchpad.
